text: Lesson 28 showed that pyodbc writes aren't permanent until commit runs. This lesson names what that actually is -- a transaction -- and builds the safe pattern you'll reuse for the rest of this course.

Everything between opening the connection and calling commit is one transaction -- all of it becomes permanent, or none of it does. If executemany fails partway through, the except block calls conn.rollback, which discards every uncommitted change, including the earlier truncate. The staging table ends up exactly as it was before the script ran.

Not every exception should be handled the same way. pyodbc.Error covers database-specific problems -- constraint violations, type mismatches, connection drops. A bare except Exception after it catches anything else, logs it, rolls back just as safely, then re-raises so the failure isn't silently swallowed.

Here's the shape Chapter 6's ETL pipeline builds its load step around: do the work inside a try, commit only on full success, roll back and re-raise on any database error, and let the caller decide what to do about a failed load.

A transaction's whole point is this all-or-nothing guarantee -- a pipeline that writes ten rows and fails on the eleventh shouldn't leave ten orphaned rows behind. And always catch the specific pyodbc.Error before a general exception, so you don't accidentally swallow something you didn't expect.

You now have every piece of database connectivity this course needs: connecting, querying into pandas, writing back, doing it safely with parameters, SQLAlchemy, and transactions. Chapter 6 puts all of it together, starting with designing a full ETL pipeline.
